title: The whispered line
hookLine: "blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom" is whispered, except on Yom Kippur
last: LIKE THE FOUR FRINGES IN ONE HAND.

cards: Stand in a synagogue at the Shema and you'll hear six words said out loud, strong, sometimes sung. Then the room goes quiet. Lips are moving, but nobody's voice carries.
A line is being said in a whisper. It's not in the Torah, and it isn't printed as part of the verse. And on one day a year, Yom Kippur, the whole room says it out loud.

teach.h: BLESSED BE THE NAME OF HIS KINGDOM.
teach.b: The line is baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed: blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever. The Talmud, in tractate Pesachim, tells where it comes from.
Jacob lies dying, his twelve sons around him. He's afraid one of them has drifted from his faith.
The sons answer with the words of the Shema, using his other name, Israel: hear, O Israel, our father, the LORD is our God, the LORD is one. Just as there is only one in your heart, so in ours.
And Jacob, relieved, answers: blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever. So the rabbis faced a puzzle. Should we say Jacob's line?
Moses didn't write it in the Torah. Should we leave it out? Jacob said it.

Their answer: say it, quietly. They compare it to a king's daughter who craved a spiced dish; to say so openly would embarrass her, to go without would hurt her, so her servants brought it to her in secret.
A midrash tells another story: Moses overheard the line from the angels and brought it down, so on most days people say it softly, as something borrowed.
But on Yom Kippur, when people are said to be like angels, they say it aloud.
It has a Temple history, too. On Yom Kippur, when the high priest spoke God's name, the crowd answered with this very line.

how: Right after the first verse of the Shema, Jews say 'blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever' in an undertone, except on Yom Kippur, when it is said aloud.

games.q: you're one of the rabbis. Jacob said this line, but Moses didn't write it in the Torah. what do you rule?
o: say it aloud with the Shema.
games.why: the Talmud rules: say it quietly, like a king's daughter's craving her servants met in secret. on Yom Kippur, it's said aloud.

practice: Think of something true you don't usually say out loud: thanks you're too shy to give, a fragile hope, love you haven't spoken. Breathe with it for a while, then whisper it, barely a breath, so only you can hear.
If you pray, you can whisper the line itself: baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed.

wordCard.voice: Baruch shem. Blessed be the name — the whispered line said right after the Shema, aloud only on Yom Kippur.
